messages.body_plain:
Hello, everyone.

I'm reading the MacKenzie et al. 2018 book in Occupancy, specifically chapter 14 on species co-occupancy. I have two questions that I hope could be answered here even though I know this group is about the unmarked package.

1. What parametrization method does unmarked uses for the occuMulti function?

2. The co-occupancy model states that species A should be the dominant species (I assume in terms of behavior and not the one suspected to be the most abundant one). So my question is what happens to the model if I switch species and use the non-dominant as species A? The reason I ask is because I am working with a two-species model and even though one of the species is considered to be more dominant, I have some areas where I have few recaptures of this dominant species and lots of the other species which is supposed to be the non-dominant between the two.

Thanks

Gabby Palomo

messages.body_plain:
Hi Gabriela,
1.As John says, the unmarked model is that of Rota et al 2016, in wich a priori no dominance of any specie is assumed over the other.
 2. The model you refer to is the reparameterization of Richmond et al 2010 which assumes one species is dominant over another, that is, species A influences the observational or ecological process of species B (eg, the wolves affect psi and p of coyotes). As this is not always true in nature, it is good to know about the ecology of both species, besides taking into account that this model only works for the interaction of two species.
The fact of having a greater number of detections (or as you said "recaptures") of the subordinate specie (B) in some areas is perfect, the objective of these models is to determine what influence the change in detection or occupation. Is it due to species A ?, the environment (covariates) ?, or both situations ?.

My English is very rough so I hope you understand me.

regards

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

we are proud to present the new Swiss breeding bird atlas:  Knaus, P., Antoniazza, S., Wechsler, S., Guélat, J., Kéry, M., Strebel, N. & Sattler, T. 2018. Brutvogelatlas 2013–2016. Bestandsentwicklung der Brutvögel der Schweiz und des Fürstentums Liechtensteins (Swiss Breeding Bird Atlas 2013–2016). Schweizerische Vogelwarte, Sempach.  See also here: https://www.vogelwarte.ch/en/projects/monitoring/swiss-breeding-bird-atlas. You can buy your copy in German or in French (the Italian version is sold out) and you can send me an email if you're interested in receiving a free pdf in any of these languages.

In addition, here you can download the English pdf of the entire atlas for free: https://www.dropbox.com/s/46s6x2tg16be3k1/SwissBreedingBirdAtlas_2013_2016.pdf?dl=0.

We think that this atlas sets new standards in several methodological ways:

--- It must be one of the first breeding bird atlases, worldwide, that attempts to produce the species abundance and distribution maps with accommodation of both imperfect detection and spatial autocorrelation (in addition to a bunch of environmental covariates) for as many species as possible (132).

--- That is, this atlas represents probably one of the biggest practical applications of the binomial N-mixture model (Royle, Biometrics, 2004) and of the site-occupancy model (MacKenzie et al., Ecology, 2002; Tyre et al.,  Ecol. App., 2003). In addition, a spatial (search-encounter) capture recapture model (Royle et al., MEE, 2011) was used for estimation of national population sizes for several dozens of the more common species.

--- And finally, this atlas demonstrates that BUGS software can be used to fit such models at a fairly large spatial scale: we used JAGS to fit all the Nmix and site-occ models, with splines for spatial autocorrelation, to the 42,000 1 km2 squares in Switzerland.

We hope that this atlas can serve as an encouragement for more widespread incorporation of a rigorous specification of the observation error in statistical analyses in biodiversity monitoring projects and in species distribution models (SDMs). We think that our atlas demonstrates that these models, which can be implemented in BUGS software, have definitely left the R&D phase and have moved on to the 'production phase.'

Best regards  ----  Marc

I created an abundance model with pcountOpen, using a negative binomial distribution and an exponential trend.
I want to check the overdispersion (alpha) to see if I should stick with NB, or whether I could also use a Poisson distribution (NB does better in terms of the AIC, but I am looking at this due to the identifiability issues of NB models mentioned in "Identifiability in N-mixture models: a large-scale screening test with bird data" (Kery, 2018). In addition, I have concerns about increasing K causing higher abundance (even though AIC seems to even out), as mentioned in a post/discussion in this group).

If I understand Hostetler and Chandler (2015) correctly, pcountOpen creates a distribution for each year (description of initial abundance on page 1715, and formula 4). But when I do
alpha <- backTransform(final_model, type="alpha")
I only get one value. Is this for the first year? Is there a way to get alpha for subsequent years?

I'm also not completely sure about the output:
 Estimate    SE    LinComb alpha
    0.529    0.369   -0.637     1
Transformation: exp

Is "estimate" the value for alpha? Then what is "alpha" in the output? What does LinComb represent?
How does it relate to this part in the summary outputs (again also one value for dispersion):
Dispersion (log-scale):
 Estimate    SE      z         P(>|z|)
   -0.637 0.698    -0.913   0.361

The help page says "lower alpha implies higher variance": should I interpret this that if alpha is high, I could potentially also use a Poisson distribution? What would be the definition of "high"? Is this compared to the data - I am modeling ticks, so have annual abundances ranging from 50 to 250 individuals per site.

Thanks in advance for any pointers, help or lit references!

And as a PS I do think I have too much heterogeneity between my sites, which has been mentioned in the literature as a possible cause for the issues I mentioned with my NB model. I have already added observation-level covariates and am working on adding more site-level covariates, which I hope might help the situation.

messages.body_plain:
Dear Dr. Klarenberg,

I think others on the group could be more helpful with many of your questions, but I'll contribute what I can.

In this model, the negative binomial distribution describes abundance in the first year (mean and overdispersion). So yes, the alpha estimate is for the first year. There may be some sort of post-hoc way to estimate overdispersion in subsequent years, but I don't know it. In your backtransformed output, "Estimate" (0.529) is the estimate of alpha. "LinComb" (-0.637) is the estimate on the log scale, which is also the estimate presented in the original output. I forget what "alpha" represents here.

What is your backtransformed estimate of mean initial abundance (lambda)? If it is indeed something in the 50-100 range, then yes, I'd say 0.529 is a very low alpha (high overdispersion). Bolker writes in his 2008 book "For k [alpha] > 10 mu [lambda], the negative binomial is hard to tell from a Poisson distribution, but k is often less than mu in ecological applications." Your idea of including site-level covariates to explain at least some of the variation in initial abundance is a good one.

Jeff

Hi Geraldine,

Those plans sound reasonable to me.

In open N-mixture models such as Dail and Madsen and our modifications, there is no explicit distribution for abundance across sites in year t, except when t=1. Instead the abundance in each site is modeled based on the abundance in that site in the previous year. In the model you're using (trend), this follows equation 4 in our paper, as you mentioned. I suppose one could, after estimating all the abundances for each site and year, see if the abundance in year t != 1 more closely matches a Poisson or NB distribution, but I'm not sure what the purpose of doing that would be. My guess is if initial abundance is modeled as NB, subsequent abundances would come out that way as well.

Jeff

Greetings, I tried to run the simulation in the book (pg.585-586). Can anyone explain why I got this error:

Error in simOcc(M = nsites[j], J = nsurveys[k], mean.occupancy = 0.5,  :
  could not find function "simOcc"

Thanks, Steve

I'm using the following versions:
R 3.5.3
‘unmarked’ 0.12-3

This is the simulation code from the book:

# Do simulation with 1000 reps
simreps <- 1000
library(unmarked)
# Define arrays to hold the results
p <- array(dim = c(simreps,3,3))
estimates <- array(dim = c(2,simreps,3,3))
# Choose number and levels of simulation factors
nsites <- c(20, 120, 250) # Number of sites
nsurveys <- c(2, 5, 10) # Number of repeat surveys
# Start simulation
system.time( # Time whole thing
  for(j in 1:3) { # Loop j over site factor
    for(k in 1:3) { # Loop k over survey factor
      for(i in 1:simreps){ # Loop i over simreps
        # Counter
        cat("** nsites", j, "nsurveys", k, "simrep", i, "***\n")
        # Generate a data set: pick p and use p in simOcc()
        det.prob <- runif(1, 0.01, 0.99)
        data <- simOcc(M = nsites[j], J = nsurveys[k], mean.occupancy = 0.5,
                       beta1 = 0, beta2 = 0, beta3 = 0, mean.detection = det.prob,
                       time.effects = c(0, 0), alpha1 = 0, alpha2 = 0, alpha3 = 0,
                       sd.lp = 0, b = 0, show.plot = F)
        # Fit model
        umf <- unmarkedFrameOccu(y = data$y)
        tmp <- occu(~1 ~1, umf, se = FALSE) # Only get MLEs, not SEs
        # Save results (p and MLEs)
        p[i,j,k] <- data$mean.det
        estimates[,i,j,k] <- coef(tmp)
      }
    }
  }
)

Dear unmarked developer,

I have collected 12 environmental covariates and wanted to get the best model to calculate the abundance. However, when I write the (~p, ~λ) part, it seems to have a huge number of possible combinations.

I think the p and λ are independent, so I try to separate the project in two runs: one is (~p, ~1) and the other is (~1, ~λ). Each run generated 4,095 possible models. Then I take the least AIC model [(~pbest, ~1) and (~1, λbest)] from each run to combine as (~pbest, ~λbest).

However, when I compare (~pbest, ~λbest) and (~1, λbest), it turns out the AIC of the latter one is smaller. I think this means potentially, there are other possible models that haven't been checked with this strategy exist. However, to run all possible combinations (4,095 x 4,095 = 16,769,025) seems not quite possible, as running 4,095 combinations took 3 days.

May I ask if there is way to efficiently get the best model?

Many thanks and best regards,

Yan

Hi Robby,

you can of course do this but must know that your estimates you get will be biased if detection probability p < 1 and if there are patterns in p in time and/or space. However, since it seems to me that in a majority of analyses in ecology, people still ignore p, I think you can do this, too, or at least, this should not be seen as a fatal flaw when you want to publish this. If this is all the data you have, then why not use it, but discuss very carefully the potential for the violation of the p<1 and the p = constant assumptions to fault the main inferences you make about your system.

Best regards  --- Marc

messages.subject: Re: parboot() and parallel processing
messages.subject_clean: parboot() and parallel processing
messages.body_plain:
This error is due to the way unmarked fits updated models with new formulas or datasets, which is required for parboot() and thus mb.gof.test(). Some unmarked helper functions can't always handle situations where the original fitted model had expressions passed as arguments, as you have with

unmarked::occu(as.formula(x[[1]]),x[[2]])

You can work around this issue in an extremely hacky way by modifying the saved `call` attribute of the unmarked fit object to trick unmarked into using the right formula and dataset. I don't have your full dataset to demonstrate but here's an example with the built in frog dataset:

data(frogs)
pferUMF <- unmarkedFrameOccu(pfer.bin)
# add some fake covariates for illustration
siteCovs(pferUMF) <- data.frame(sitevar1 = rnorm(numSites(pferUMF)))
# observation covariates are in site-major, observation-minor order
obsCovs(pferUMF) <- data.frame(obsvar1 = rnorm(numSites(pferUMF) * obsNum(pferUMF)))

mods <- list(
             list(formula='~1~1',data=pferUMF),
             list(formula='~obsvar1~1', data=pferUMF)
             )

run_um <- function(x){unmarked::occu(as.formula(x[[1]]),x[[2]])} #here is where the issue comes in

cl <- makeCluster(detectCores()-1)

mods_out <- parLapply(cl=cl, X=mods, run_um)

#GOF

#Would need to change pferUMF here to your dataset name
clusterExport(cl, c('pferUMF', 'mods', 'mods_out'))

run_gof <- function(i){

  #Modify call attribute of the model to work around issue
  new_call <- call('occu',as.formula(mods[[i]][[1]]),mods[[i]][[2]])

  this_mod <- mods_out[[i]]
  this_mod@call[2] <- new_call[2]
  this_mod@call[3] <- new_call[3]

  #Don't want to set this to parallel also, as you are
  #already in a parallel loop

messages.subject_clean: Dynocc multi-season model error bar problem
messages.body_plain:
Hey everyone!

I am applying multi-season dynamic occupancy models to large mammal species in Turkey by using single-species camera trapping data.

I have a problem by having full error bars (from 0 to 1) for some species depending on various variables and I couldn't figure it out the problem. Since my detection history (presences) are relatively sparse, I decided to build models with 2 different environmental variables at a time for one population parameter. I selected the final model by trying out all of the variables and based on their AIC comparisons.

For example for S.scrofa species, the final model is selected as:

library(unmarked)

sscrofa <-unmarkedMultFrame(y = data1,
                            siteCovs = data.frame(habitat=habitat, province=province, town=town,
                                                  elevation=elevation, slope=slope, aspect=aspect),
                            yearlySiteCovs = list(season=season),numPrimary = 6)

dm_sscrofa <- colext(psiformula = ~ province,
                     gammaformula = ~ season + elevation + season:elevation,
                     epsilonformula = ~ season + province + season:province,
                     pformula = ~ slope,
                     data = sscrofa)

and when I try to get the results for colonization (gamma -  whis is affected by season, elevation and their interaction) with predict function the outcome is:

nd_col <- expand.grid(season=c('S', 'W'), elevation = seq(-2.489484, 1.321115, length.out = 6))  # this is the new data set for predict function, S for summer and W for winter

dat_col = cbind(nd_col,predict(dm_sscrofa, type='col', newdata=nd_col)) # this is the final result with covariates and predicted means, used for plot

ggplot(dat_col,aes(elevation,Predicted,col=season,group=season))+
  geom_point(position = position_dodge(width = 0.5))+
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), width = 0.2, position = position_dodge(width = 0.5))+
  ylab('Colonization')

Why do I get this full error bars when I predict results from the model?
Additionally, if the effect of elevation is this bad to the gamma, why is this model selected among others as the best parsimonious model?

Any help would be appreciated.

Thank you,
Dilsad

messages.body_plain:
Dear Dilsad,

looking at the estimates, I note that both point estimates and SEs are extremely large (in absolute terms). This suggests that something has gone wrong in the estimation. From your umf summary one can see that your data set does not seem to be too sparse, but nevertheless, I think that your model may be too complex for it. Try a step-up model buildin strategy, starting with the simplest model (with 4 intercepts) and then adding covariates one by one. Not as a formal strategy of model selection, but just to be better able to diagnose the source for numerical problems in fitting the model. As soon as you get such extremely large point estimates and/or SEs, you know that the term added last causes this problem.

Indeed, AIC can select a model with useless estimates, for instance, in the context of the binomial N-mixture model, AIC often tells you that a model with Negative binomial abundance mixture fits best, by far, and yet it predicts totally unrealistically high levels of abundance. To be honest, I don't fully understand this (OK, it may be due to boundary estimates, see also Dennis et al., Biometrics, 2015 and Kery, Ecology, 2018). But perhaps one thing to learn from this is: the best-fitting model is not necessarily the model that you should use. But I digress....

So, try that step-up modeling strategy. And remember that you don't need to try out all possible covariate combinations in your model, or even many variables, to be a good scientist. Some respectable people say that you can just build a single model, which makes sense to you based on what you know about the system, on your available data and your questions. See this paper:  https://wildlife.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/jwmg.891

Best regards  --- Marc

messages.body_plain:
Dear Yan,

What capture-recapture and occupancy people usually do is a sequential approach to model selection: first optimize one part of the model using AIC, then keep the ‘optimal’ structure for that and proceed to optimizing the other part of the model. Typically, people start with the detection part, keeping the survival or occupancy part reasonably general (probably better than keeping it constant), and then keep the best structure for detection and optimize survival or occupancy (or abundance in your case).

That approach is of course not guaranteed to find the overall AIC-best model, but it seems to be a useful pragmatic approach that is widely used.

Best regards  --- Marc

turnover <- function(fm) {

  psi.hat <- plogis(coef(fm, type="psi"))

  T <- getData(fm)@numPrimary
  tau.hat <- numeric(T-1)

  gamma.hat <- plogis(coef(fm, type="col"))

  phi.hat <- 1 - plogis(coef(fm, type="ext"))

  if(length(gamma.hat) != T-1 | length(phi.hat) != T-1)

    stop("this function only works if gamma and phi T-1 vectors")

  for(t in 2:T) {

    psi.hat[t] <- psi.hat[t-1]*phi.hat[t-1] +

      (1-psi.hat[t-1])*gamma.hat[t-1]

    tau.hat[t-1] <- gamma.hat[t-1]*(1-psi.hat[t-1]) / psi.hat[t]
  }

  return(tau.hat)
}

Thanks

Yan,

I don't believe the p and λ portions of the hierarchical distance sampling model fit by unmarked::distsamp are independent.  You might look at a Bromaghin et al. 2013 paper (https://www.scirp.org/journal/PaperInformation.aspx?PaperID=27677) that provides an alternative model-selection process (called "Plausible Combinations") for cases like yours (i.e., cases where there are multiple submodels [p and λ] and you want to explore multiple covariates for each).  The authors compared this Plausible Combinations approach to the sequential approaches Marc mentioned, and an all-possible combinations approach.

Jason

Dear Yan,

According to the papers I read, none of them have reach such a high number of covariates. Some papers stated that they tested all possible combinations of covariates but more papers didn't mention they did so.

There is one recently published paper by Valenzuela-Sánchez et al. ("Assessing habitat quality when forest attributes have opposing effects on abundance and detectability: A case study on Darwin’s frogs"), mentioned an alternative of a two-stage ad hoc strategy.

I tried the strategy but it seems there is very high chance that the best model is still hiding in the possible combinations untested by the strategy.

My conclusion is that you have to try all the possible combinations to get the best model. Otherwise you may need an excuse for not testing all of them.

Best,

Q

messages.body_plain:
Dear Qian,

I beg to differ: for better or worse, I don't think that you actually need to check out all possible combinations if you want to get your paper published. Over the past couple of years I must have seen dozens of papers who employed the sequential approach (and I am guilty of some of them myself). I am not saying that this is necessarily the best approach, but I just don't think that referees necessarily reject your paper if you do something other than the all-combinations approach, if this would involve fitting more than, say, 50-100 models.

And as a personal side comment: I think that model selection in the sense of a blind hunt for the lowest-AIC model is overrated anyway. I am not against trying to find one with an as low AIC as you can get, but don't spend sleep-less nights over the risk that you may have missed a model with even lower AIC. For two and a half reasons: first, there will always exist many, many models with lower AIC than the one you found (for instance, if you could get 'real good' explanatory variables, not the cheap proxies that you have). And second, because there are certainly cases where a model with dramatically low AIC can be totally useless, cf. in the case of many Nmix models with Negative binomial as opposed to a Poisson abundance mixture (see Kery, Ecology, 2018). And finally, there is much more to model selection than AIC-ology, see e.g. the monograph by Hooten & Hobbs (2015).

Side comment 2: I am not against model selection: I would do as good as I can, but at the same time remain somewhat relaxed about it.

Best regards  --- Marc

Subject: [unmarked] Re: distsamp() modeling with many covariates

Dear Yan,

According to the papers I read, none of them have reach such a high number of covariates. Some papers stated that they tested all possible combinations of covariates but more papers didn't mention they did so.

There is one recently published paper by Valenzuela-Sánchez et al. ("Assessing habitat quality when forest attributes have opposing effects on abundance and detectability: A case study on Darwin’s frogs"), mentioned an alternative of a two-stage ad hoc strategy.

I tried the strategy but it seems there is very high chance that the best model is still hiding in the possible combinations untested by the strategy.

My conclusion is that you have to try all the possible combinations to get the best model. Otherwise you may need an excuse for not testing all of them.

Best,

Q

messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I have (what I think is) a quick question regarding the pcountOpen function.

I am using the function to fit open population abundance models in multiple sites and in up to 33 surveying occasions (biweekly measurements) for mosquito captures.  The closed population assumption does not hold in my case, so having the parameters for the recruitment rate (gamma) and survival probability (omega) vary in time would make sense (e.g., temperature will affect recruitment and survival). So, is it possible in the code to incorporate observation level covariates for the gamma and omega parameters?

Any information will be greatly appreciated!

Daniel
